projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Arthur Gedeon was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Arthur W. Gedeon. Art served in the U.S. Army Air Corps 585th Bomb Squadron. He served in the European Theater and in India. His highest rank was tech sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at my home in Mentor, Ohio, on June 9, 2001. Art was 81 at the time of this recording. Question: Do you remember when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor? Do you remember where you were?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Where the hell was I?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was in December, '41.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You -- Where did that put you? You were 21. Were you working then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yes. Yeah, I was working then. I'm trying to think where the heck I -- where was I? Don't -- Don't get --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is all right. _________ out the tape.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I'm trying to think. Where the hell was I? '41. I think -- I think I was home or I was out and I came home and Mae --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Mae told me, she says --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: We were living off West 48th Street.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Down -- Down below Dennison Avenue. We were living down there when they attacked.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Or whatever.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you wait to be drafted or did you go out and enlist?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No. Believe it or not, the company held me out two or three different times 'cause of the job, right? And then I knew I was going to be drafted right after the first of the year; so I went down to the mall downtown and that's where they take -- you know, gung ho, I was going to try to get in on the Marines. So I went down there, talked to the fella, and they checked everything and -- and my -- my right eye has a little coloring in it, you know. And -- So he said, "Go get it checked." So I went to the mall, got it checked; I come back, gave him the slip; he said, "Oh, you're okay then." He said, "You can leave." I said, "When will I leave?" He said, "Before Christmas." And we had just been married in April. I says, "No way." He says, "You either go now or you don't go." I says, "Well, I guess I don't go." And it worked out right for me because I came -- right after the first of the year, I got my "Helloooo," you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And then -- then I left. I left after that. It worked out good. I mean, I went down -- down to Columbus; and then from there I went -- I went down to Miami, stopped at a place -- I went down to Miami for basic training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What job were you working that you got the deferments?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Machine tool building. We were building grinders, polishers that -- in fact, we started making small -- small, 6 foot grinders that they took on the ships with them for repair work. You know, if they -- something broke down on the ship that they needed some grinding or something, they had it on the ship to do it with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And it did -- They kept me out three times. Yeah, really. They kept me out of there three different times. I did go three times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you would have gone in then -- So you were drafted, right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I was drafted. I ended up being --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: January '43.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, right. I was actually drafted then. Because, like I said, I tried to get into the Marines but, tough, I wasn't going to go before -- before Christmas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: 'Cause we had just gotten married -- well, April, May, June, July, you know; so it worked out good though. And it worked out good for me too. I mean, I came back, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I came back. The plane was shot up but we made it back. All of us made it back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Mac, the engineer on the top turret, his knee was shot up pretty bad. We left him in -- in England when we headed back stateside when we were through flying. He came back after that. And then -- Mac, we hadn't seen him for years; and then Mae was cleaning out the drawers and everything and she seen his name, you know, John Mackie (ph), Virginia City; and I says, "You know what, Hon, I wonder if he's home or if he's gone someplace." 'Cause we lost touch with him after he was in the hospital. We had this stateside. And -- So I wrote a little note. This is Virginia City, Minnesota.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I wrote a little note and I said, "Mac, if you're alive, get in touch with me. This is my phone number." And, fortunately, his sister worked in the post office up there in Virginia City; and she says, "Mac, do you know an Art Gedeon?" He said, "Hell, yeah," he says, "I flew with him." She says, "Well, there's a letter here for you." He called me the same night, yeah, when he got it. He called me the same night and then he called and we went out there. I think it was about five, six weeks later. Yeah. He had a jewelry store up there. Sucker did good. He started off first -- when he came back stateside, he started off in the grocery business, he and his wife, with a restaurant and that and that was too much work and then -- then he went to the GI for the jewelry deal, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And he -- he ended up -- There was three jewelers in Virginia City -- it's a small little place, you know. And he ended up -- he bought 'em all out. He was there by himself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. The sucker he -- he still drank.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You started going into your training there. Do you remember anything about that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You went to Columbus to train first; is that right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Four days, you said?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Four days, Columbus, yeah. And then from there I went to -- four days. Then I went to gunnery school. That was in Texas --Laredo, Texas, that's right. I went to gunnery school in Laredo, Texas. And there we -- we had gunnery every day and we had to be able to take the .50 caliber machine gun apart and put it back together; and then, in order to pass, you had a blindfold -- you had to take all apart and put it down; they mixed the parts up and you had to feel your way around, put it back together again; and then you got your wings, you know, for flying. And then from there I -- I headed down to _______, what the heck -- I'm trying to think of it. Sheffield, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Went down there for training in radio and I finished that up. I got a -- I got a permit for that or -- I guess it's called a permit or whatever, you know -- certificate; same as -- same as for the flying -- fighting -- the gunnery. Mae came down there and stayed with me. She -- She could come out to the base in the evening. Can you imagine 15 cents for a pint of ice-cream? Oh, we were young. We sat there. Got a pint of ice-cream. We -- She took off and headed back to -- she was down there for about darn near three months. And she said, "I better get a job," she says. So she -- She went out, she got herself a job. The following week, I shipped out. I went up to Battle Creek, Michigan. And up at Battle Creek, we -- we got our group together. They had formed down -- down in Atterberry; but the guys that hadn't been down there, they came up there, my pilot and copilot, all them; we -- we met each other up at -- Battle Creek, Michigan, at -- at the Kellogg Field up there. And then when we met each other, then we went in as a crew, you know. And I'll never forget this one time, our bombadier Heisan (ph) -- we were all young. I was old; I was 21. And the young -- The pilot was only 19 or 20, something like that; and Mac and I were about the oldest. But, anyway, we were going on a bomb run over Scott Field. They had up far enough -- And this was at nighttime, night bombing. And they had flour bags you dumped out, you know, the bombadier. You open the bomb bay chute and dump the bombs. And I'll never forget this. We're flying around at nighttime out there and Ryerson (ph), the pilot, he says, "Okay, Hei (ph)," he says, "take over now." He said, "It's your plane." He says, "Put the -- Put the bombs where they belong." And he opened the bomb bay doors and Ryerson (ph) says, "Heisan (ph), are you sure you know what you're doing?" Hei (ph) said, "Yeah." He said, "I got the damn thing in my face." He says, "That isn't it," he says, "that's Kellogg's corn flakes down there." This is no lie. But eventually Heisan (ph) became one of the lead -- lead navigators.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you drop it on Kellogg's?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No. No. He didn't. Ryerson (ph) stopped him. But he did -- He became one -- one of the group's lead -- leading navigators and bombadiers. And see, when we got overseas then, we didn't have enough -- actually lieutenant bombadiers, navigators, you know; so we had togaliers (ph), they called them. They were regular sergeants and -- GIs like me. And they would bomb off the first -- first ship or number 4 ship, the lead ship or, you know, 4 ship. They opened the bomb bay doors same time as they did; and when the bombs started out, they pushed a button, they dumped our bombs too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you just followed the lead of whoever was in front of --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, right. When we were flying lead ship or number 4, we had an extra guy on the crew. I was a radio operator then. And then we had an extra guy at the waist guns. Otherwise, I was strictly a waist gunner.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And it worked out right. We -- We were -- Most of our kills -- our kills on the planes and everything was through flak. Because at that time our fighters were doing pretty doggone good and our bomb -- the 17 and 24s, they were taking a beatin', not -- not the 26s, you know; we were medium. We were in and out for four hours, that's all. These guys would be up there for an eight-hour spell. I felt sorry for them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you bombing targets mainly in France then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. France, Belgium. We -- We went into Germany but not -- not far. In across the Rhine River and places like that we were hitting -- we were hitting targets. And before D-day, we were hitting flak towers and everything else. And we were bombing along the -- on the shoreline, all the -- the gun emplacements that they had set up there -- _______ set up there. We were bombing them too. I remember one time, near Rouen, we were supposed to take out a bridge just prior to the invasion and they didn't want the Germans to bring any supplies across; and we were -- we were -- we were up about 6, 7,000 feet and making a bomb run. There's a Frenchman on a bicycle down there. That's how they traveled, you know. And he's pumping his butt off. He wants to get across that damn bridge in the worst way, you know, he kind of figured they were going to blow it up. And I -- I threw some shots down toward him -- I seen where the tracers went -- just to scare him so he wouldn't go across. But he made -- He made the end of the bridge, and the bridge went. They got the bridge. And I tell you, they were getting pretty doggone good. On the other side of the bridge, in Rouen itself, there's a big church there, a beautiful church; and all they did was get beat up a little bit from the -- from the missiles, you know, all the junk blowing up; but they never bombed the church. So I'm -- I'm telling you, they were -- they were getting good. They were getting good. Our boys, they'd learned. Going overseas, I was the only one of the crew that went -- I mean, outside of the pilot and copilot and -- we had an engineer that went along 'cause then we flew -- we flew down to Florida. We flew to Ascension Islands. And from there we went over to Barmetz (ph), England, and I was the only guy on the crew. And at nighttime, I'd sit out and guard the plane. On Ascension Island, who the heck's going to go there? But I guess that was war.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were the only one, other than the pilot, that was on that -- when the plane went over?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Plane went over, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there what, a pilot, copilot, and you ___?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Engineer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Engineer.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And an engineer too, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And it wasn't Mackie (ph). It was a flight engineer, you know, that would really work on the planes when we -- when we brought 'em back. He -- He was -- He came with us. I called him Jingle Buckets (ph). I can't re -- call him Barney or something like that was his name. He was an Italian fella and -- he was good. That plane held up good for us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you based in England?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Warmouth (ph). Right outside of Chelmsford. And for a while there, when they were starting -- Germans started sending these buzz bombs over, they -- they were going for Chelmsford and there was a ball bearing factory there and you could see these doggone -- oh, what the hell do you call them -- V2s?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: V2s?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: V2s, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: They'd come right across our field. Honest to goodness. And -- And, you know, they come in low, you hear them run out of gas and, varoom, that was it. I know many a time we were in London, we got a forty-eight-hour pass, we'd go into London, we'd stay at the hotel there; and at nighttime you'd hear them damn things stooging (ph) over, and, boom. That's when they were bombing the heck out of London at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: You'd go down in the tubes, the subways down there, all the people were sleeping down in there, you know. London took a beatin'. Actually -- Actually, so did Germany at the end.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But London -- London took a pastin'. The one time we went over to the E-Boat pens in Holland, the sub pens that the Germans had over there. They -- They -- They would always have these German subs, like a pack of so many would go -- go out into the Atlantic and that and knock all this stuff that United States was sending overseas, you know; and we lost -- we lost a lot of plane -- boats. But that one time they told us, "We must stay down low." I was up in the water. The radar would pick us up. Well, that was true. They did pick us up. They could see us. So they just leveled their guns. We lost more -- more guys that day because the minute they were hit, they were in the water. At least in the air, when you were hit, you stood a little chance. Not much. But you stood a chance, you know. And so we -- We took a pastin' that day, the whole outfit did, 'cause the 394ths -- well, we had -- 585th, we had 15 -- close -- close to, altogether, I think, about 50, 60 planes altogether, you know; and we -- we took a beatin' that day. Another time we took a beating is on our way back, and we were coming in for a landing, and a couple of Germans followed us in. When we got on this side of the Channel, we usually stored our guns. That was the last time we stored our guns. 'Cause two of the planes came down, shot the heck out of the guys that were making the landing. We had no defense. You know, that was dumb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: It was a dumb as a blunder. It was a dumb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was standard procedure to do that then.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: We did it, you know. We'd -- We'd get on this -- We'd get on the England side and we'd pull our guns in, sit around, bullshit. That's what it amounted to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have other specific memories about D-day? Arthur W. Gedeon June 9, 2001

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well, just prior to D-day, we'd wonder what the heck was happening 'cause they started painting our planes we were flying. They had the white stripes on 'em. So we recognized each other actually. And then -- Man, I'll tell you, the ships in the Channel, you won't believe how many were there. And the planes in the air, you know. I mean, cripes, it surprised that they didn't run into each other. I imagine some of them probably did but what a -- what a beautiful thing to see, all these planes, all these boats down there. And they took a beatin' too, you know. Oh, you've seen -- I mean, D-day there, our boys took a poundin'. But, no, it -- it worked out pretty good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What -- What -- Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What time did you go out on D-day then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Twice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You went out twice?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Twice, yeah. We -- We went in the morning. They woke us up, I think it was about 2:30, 3:00, something like that. We went in and tried to knock out the flak towers and gun emplacements along the -- along the shore. Came back, had something to eat, they re -- refixed the planes, make sure we have fuel and ammunition and everything, went back again in the afternoon. At that time, our guys were already on the beach or making progress. But the first time we went in was low. And then our fighters -- We had fighters all over the place. They were our boys, you know. At that time, actually, the Germans, they didn't have much of an air force any more but they pulled ahead -- they was doing good; but them boys were -- I'll never forget the one time -- Connie sat in the tail, tail turret; and every time we -- some plane would blow -- blow up or crash or something like that, he'd always scrounge over and get some metal and put around the back end so all he could -- get his hands around by the guns, that's all he could do; but one time we were out and we were flying -- let's see, there was 12 ships above us. We were the next flight down. And we had P47 escorts that got a big nacelle on it and their _____ 190s, they had a big nacelle on them. And after we had tested our guns, once we -- once we got out in the Channel, we're heading in towards our target, and Connie, the tail gunner, he says, "Ry," he says, "look at -- look at that asshole coming down with his landing lights on." There was a fighter coming down with his -- firing, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And he says, "Look at him." He says, "Sam," he says, "that's not our instruction _______." I imagine you cut out what you don't --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: It was -- It's things like that you remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: It's oddball things. Oh, cripes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So would it have been that second time you went out when you hit that bridge?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That bridge over Rouen, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. We hit that sucker.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your -- your group, did you do a lot of low-level bombing then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well, we started -- We didn't go over 10,000. Once or twice we went over 10,000 feet. Then we had to go on oxygen. Everything else was scattered down from like 9,500, 7,800. They staggered them down so we didn't have to go on oxygen. Like the heavies, they were on oxygen damn near all the time, you know. Them boys, they took a poundin'. The only poundin' we took was, more or less, from flak. We did get a lot of shell -- knock -- guys knocked down with the airplanes, you know, with the fighters -- their fighters; but most of ours was flak that got us. And we wore flak suits and -- I guess they got them now on the police department, you know, little flakes in them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And at one time, when -- the time Mac got hit, I had pieces stuck in my flak suit; so I would have got hit too, only, fortunately, I had the suit on. But in that turret where he was, that poor soul, he's sittin' up there all by his lonesome, and ammunition all around him; so when -- when it hit there, he -- some of the ammunition let go and it got his knees; but -- but he got 10 percent; so it wasn't -- wasn't all that bad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So tell -- tell the story, I think we told it before, but go ahead and tell the story when -- when I think it was Mac that got hit and you were giving him medical attention.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. This is no lie. Mac was hit. The only way he can get out of that damn thing is if I or somebody lets him out 'cause he couldn't reach around; he was hurt. I dropped him down and we had these Syrettes, these morphine Syrettes. The first thing I did was, "How you doin', Mackie (ph)?" "I'm okay." I took a Syrette, I gave him a shot -- a shot of morphine. And then we -- we had a lull in the -- in the -- on the flak and Connie hollered back, "How's he doing?" I said, "Not bad." He -- He came back out of the tail end. And he says, "Oh, heck," he says, "he's suffering." He took a Syrette and he gave him a Syrette. My pilot hollered down, he said, "How's he doing?" We said, "Oh, he's doing pretty good." He says -- He told Heisan (ph), he says, "Heisan (ph), give him a little morphine; he might need it." That guy could have become an addict or die. We could have killed him, you know. But it could help him. It didn't hurt him. I mean, well, it didn't help him; but he didn't feel it, let's put it that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The pain went away.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: That's exactly right. The pain went away.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But -- No, that's it. That's it. We were fortunate. That's all I can say, Tommy. You know, really, we were lucky. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As a waist gunner, do you remember hitting anything?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I don't know. I shot at 'em. But I don't know if -- All you have was you had a tracer, armor piercing, and -- what the hell is the one that ignites?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, whatever they're -- incendiary.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Incendiary, right, right. So every third one was a tracer. So you could see where your bullets were going, you know. And the only way you could get -- well, if they were coming at you, you had a chance of shooting at it. They were going by, you had to lead them like crazy because they're -- whew, they went right by. And we did -- Towards the end there, just before I stopped flying, we seen the -- the jet. The Germans, remember, they started coming out with the jets? Why, had they come out with them damn things sooner, we would have taken a pastin'. But -- And he went zhew, just like that. Like you -- You wouldn't believe it. Well, like the jets today. You know, you don't believe it, the speed that they got. And -- I don't know how the heck to say it but we were fortunate. Sam -- Mac was the only one that got hurt and we all came back. We all come back stateside. And we come back -- We come back in the old Dutch boat. In the morning, they'd reveil -- reveille us out, 0600 hours. We'd eat -- We had good food on that doggone boat; but, you know, the funny part was, it was -- it wasn't all Air Force that was on the boat either. It was good -- good number of the -- the boys on the ground, you know, the foot soldiers; and they weren't used -- used to the tossing and turning of the boat. First day, everybody was down there; they had good food; and it was good food they served. The next day, I don't think there was half of them down there. Most of them was Air Force guys because their stomachs were used to this. These poor souls, they were sick.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. They're used to real food.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, they was sick. It -- It worked out real well for us, though. I'm thankful. We -- We come back. Quite -- Well, like your dad, he -- he ended up in the concentration camp, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Do you -- Do you know if any of your buddies, anybody from the group, that was --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: A couple of them did. One -- One of them, he lived off of Storr (ph) Avenue and he was a -- he was a tail gunner and they -- they had to bail out. The plane was shot up pretty badly. He had to bail out. They bailed out. He was taken prisoner. And he has called me once after that, but then they moved. But -- I guess they got treated, such as they could, you know. They abided by the Geneva Convention as much as they could too. Not like the Japanese now. The Japanese, they -- they didn't give a damn one way or the other.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I was trying to think now. What the heck was it? Oh, yeah. Well, then I came -- then I came back stateside. Oh, yeah. Mae had had the kid. We were all through flying in France. And Mae -- Mae had Eileen then, and I got this three weeks after she had the kid already. Anyway, when we did get home, I stayed home; I -- I -- I had furlough coming. I was back home and I wrote down -- going down -- going down to Florida. And I sent her a telegram. When I never got an answer, I wrote and never got answer. I took off, went down there on my -- on my discharge papers, three days AWOL. Yeah, I got up the Colonel -- got up by the Colonel there and he says, "Well," he says, I'm a family man," he says, "I can understand why you wanted to be home with the kid," he said, "but that's no excuse." And he says, "We did get your acknowledgment that you -- you weren't coming back right away," he said, "but we can't run this thing this way." He was nice about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: He says, "I've got to dock you." I says, "That's no problem." That's all he did though, so it worked out good. So then, went down there; and from there, I went up to Reno, Nevada; got a refresher course in radio. This is a funny one. We had H -- B26 -- not B26 -- C46s --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And they had radio equipment in them. And we took off at nighttime and went up there and they sent us signals from the ground and we'd write it down and we'd send back to them. This one night, must have been eight or ten of us, got on a plane, sat down, plane was running down the runway, and the one engine quit. He pulled around, came back, sat there, started up the engine and started running. Everybody, "Hold it." We opened the door; we got out. He took off by himself. The next day, we were all up by the Colonel. He says, "You know," he says, "they went up." We says, "Yeah, but we didn't want to get killed." So it worked out there. From there, I went back over -- I went to Karachi and then to -- yeah, Karachi; we landed in Karachi. And then I'm trying to think of the name of that little burg we went to. We were flying across -- across -- across -- across the Hump - across the Himalayas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Burma Hump, right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, we were -- we were flying over the Burma Hump.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I can't see it. Must not have mentioned it the last time.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't see it here.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, we flew over there. And then when Germany surrendered, I come back on points.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: You had to have so many points. For every mission, I got a point. So I had 66 points right there. And then we came back stateside; and I'm still -- that bugs me I can't think of the doggone place; but, anyway, we were coming across the Hump back -- back in -- back across Burma and that. The English had gun emplacements down there. They were shooting them doggone things up. They -- Celebrating because Germany had surrendered. Yeah. But nothing happened. I mean, just --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were they close?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I don't know. They were off in the distance. But we -- Yeah, we were flying obsolete planes actually over -- the old 24s, the old 17s that came from Europe. They send them over there to fly supplies over to China, you know. And we did, we flew over the Hump into China. And that -- That's -- That was precarious because you had fog so bad, clouds so bad that you couldn't land; they'd stagger them, you know, like couple hundred feet apart distance. And then I know the one time we were circling. They'd -- They'd let you keep circling till they let you down to the next level. And naturally, Ryerson's (ph) paying attention 'cause he's flying the damn thing; and they were letting another plane down from up above us, down on our -- and you should have heard Ryerson (ph). "Hey," he says, "you got to stop that," he says, "we're circling down here; we don't need anybody else down here circling with us." And I'll tell you what, them Chinese, they're working fools. They -- They worked on them there airstrips like you wouldn't believe, crushing the rock and everything else. They didn't have the equipment like we had, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you go up there with your same pilot then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were the only one --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I was the only one --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- that went?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, I was the only one of the crew that went back overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: They needed radio operators. I was the only married man too. Yeah, I was the only married man too and -- yeah, I was a radio operator. I'll never forget one time we were back in the States here. It was for Thanksgiving dinner. We were up at Battle Creek. And Mae stayed with this couple at the house there and Ryerson (ph) wanted to go -- he lived in Maryland and he wanted to go home for Thanksgiving dinner. I ended up flying with him 'cause he needed a radio operator. And Mae, she was supposed to go with me out to the field and have dinner out there, Thanksgiving dinner. Well, it worked out right, though. The couple, they took Mae in and had -- she had dinner with them. But you can imagine how she felt. I felt lousy too _______+_______. And the beauty of it was, the sucker, he didn't -- he didn't invite me up to the house or nothing like that. I -- I had to go out and shift for myself.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But, hey, it's over with. We come back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were flying -- flying supplies over the Burma Hump that _______?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long were you doing that? When did you get over there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Jesus, I don't -- I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Would it have been --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I'd have to -- I'd have to look.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: _____ maybe?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: It -- It might have been. It was prior to -- prior to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: VE-day.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: -- VE-day, yeah, okay. It was prior to that. It was prior to that time and -- yes, it was prior -- yeah, 'cause VE-day we were over there. It was prior to that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And I was the only one that had to go back overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember approximately when you got to Europe? You went in in '43.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So do you think you got there maybe early '44?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, here, you've got it written here. England and France, nine months.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you probably left -- Did you leave maybe at the end of '44?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. We got it right after -- well, before the holidays -- after the holidays, after Christmas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After Christmas.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: After Christmas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So probably January of '44.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, because we couldn't fly for a while. The weather was so bad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But then once -- once the weather started clearing, we were flying constantly. Every day they were going up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were probably -- Were you stateside for a few months before you went to Burma?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: One month.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just one month.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Just -- Just when I -- Just when I come back from overseas, I was home with Mae. Then I went down -- down to Florida. Yeah. Then from there I went out to Reno, Nevada.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Refresher course. And then shipped back out over, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many missions did you fly in Europe?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That -- In Europe?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: In Europe.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That total?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: They were all total.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 66 in Europe?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Europe, yeah; and the ones over the Hump, I never kept track. It's probably -- They probably have a record of it, you know. But I never, no. I know it was 66 in Europe though, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shouldn't you have gone home after 50?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well, yeah, you were supposed to. Well, it was the same thing with the heavies, they were supposed to go, too, right away, you know 'cause they were out longer than we were; and, yeah, they -- they said 25, then 50. They didn't -- They didn't have replacements or they didn't want to replace, I don't know what. But we stayed there. I put in 66. And we were in France. That was after D-day. We moved in France. The engineers had gone in, graded it, and put down this wire mesh, you know, this landing stripping. And then I had a good deal. I was sergeant of the guards at nighttime out there. I posted these guards; and then throughout the night, every once in a while, I'd swing by, see how things were going. And, boy, I'll tell you, when the -- when the cook -- we had a Chinese cook. He could make pancakes like you wouldn't believe. When he had pancakes, I was there every night. What happened, one time, they -- they were flying missions from -- from France off of this stripping. And this one -- The one plane, the one engine quit on them; naturally loaded with bombs. And they took off a couple seconds or so staggered behind each other. And he rolled; he blew up -- he blew up the runway; and all of them got killed. A couple other planes got beat up too. But, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Whereabouts in France was that base?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Not too far from -- I don't even know if I've got the doggone thing. It wasn't too far from -- from Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Because we had gotten a forty-eight-hour pass and went into London; and on the way back, they dropped us off in Paris. They -- They weren't going back to the field. So we spent the night in Paris; then the next day we hitched a ride and got back to our base; so it couldn't have been too far away from Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do in Paris?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, we had a good time that night. But we -- All our money was gone already because we had been in London, you know; and we had cigarettes left. And I'll never forget this -- I told Mae about this too -- they had houses of ill repute, you know; and we went in this one. It looked like a big dance hall, damn near, tables set up. And -- So there was Mac, me, and Connie. We sat down at this table. And we had enough money to buy a bottle of Calvedos (ph) and we had some cigarettes. We sat down and three girls sat down, you know. What the hell? We ain't got this kind of money. And -- Anyway -- Anyway, we ordered a bottle. And they said, "No, two bottles." We couldn't understand them. So we -- We paid -- paid with cigarettes. And then -- And then the one girl, she was putting her hands on Sam's knee, sitting next to him like that, and he kept pushing her hand away. But nothing happened. We just -- We just spent a couple hours, you know, drinking and smoking, sitting there; and then we took off. The next day we took off, we went back to the base; and then we headed back stateside.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: There was -- When we were through flying -- we -- we were through flying in England and then we moved over with the whole gang, then, after that. But there was a couple chicken farms right near us and they had big fences around these chickens. And the last -- last mission we went on, we come home and Ryerson (ph) stood that doggone thing up, you know; and he gunned the heck out of it and these chickens flying up. And he was reprimanded. He was reprimanded. "You're killing the chickens." Let's see, what the heck else can I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Celebrating, huh. So he knew it was the last one?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. We all knew that. We -- We were back. That was it. Mac wasn't with us that day. We had another one. 'Cause he was in the hospital then. But, yeah, we -- we were happy we were going. Then when we got on a boat, come back stateside, we had good food.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you were based in France there, do you remember or have any strong memories of any of those missions? Were those into Germany then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well, I -- I wasn't on them anymore. I was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, when you went over to France, you weren't --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I was through flying.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Ah. So you didn't have to --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But we had -- We had to go over with the whole outfit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You still went to France --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- even though you didn't fly?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Even if I didn't fly, that's right, yeah. And -- Well, they -- they were going in a little further into Germany, you know. Oh, I know. One time -- No, that's right -- That one time we went to the _______ -- Forest of Hesden. That's when Patton was chasing across Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And we -- We were supposed to bomb -- They said that they had, in the forest, they had German artillery and soldiers and that -- that we were supposed to bomb -- demolition bombs. And we went and we dropped these bombs, but Patton had gotten there already. And they never gave us a recall. Our planes were dropping bombs on our own guys, you know. But I guess that happens. Fortunately, it wasn't us. But, yeah, that -- that was it then. I was through over there then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that during the Normandy breakout?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, when they were going across, yeah. When they were getting -- getting out of the Bulge there. They -- They went through there. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was this during the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: This was -- This was right after, yeah, during the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And Patton, he -- he -- he just went like crazy, man. They couldn't -- They couldn't keep up with the supplies for him. I guess he was a good General and everything but, you know, he had his own way of doing things. And really we should have gotten a recall, you know; we kept dropping bombs down in there; it was a force of his. And I'll never forget that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where was that? In France or Belgium?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, that -- I think that was in Germany.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it in Germany?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: In Germany -- or -- into France, I don't know. Don't quote me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's all right there together anyway.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Close -- So close, yeah. It wasn't far. I know that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Our guys went back to France here fifteen, twenty years ago. I never did go. I never did want -- I never had the money. Let's face it. What the hell. You had to have some money to go back overseas and bum around over there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about getting letters from Mae?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I got them. And I'd send her letters too. But they were always cut up. They -- They'd delete what they didn't want you to know. Mae found out -- I -- We knew a fella by the name of Otto Furst (ph). This is fact. And I told Mae before -- before we started flying, I says, "When I tell you Otto Furst (ph) -- I seen Otto Furst(ph)," I says, "you know I started flying." And she knew when I started flying overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And he -- Otto got in the service. Older guy -- Well, Bob wasn't in. He had --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Got bad ears, yeah. And Lenny wasn't in. I guess he had bad knees.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, was Otto Furst (ph) overseas in Europe too?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, he was overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you actually see him at any point?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I never seen -- Never --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't have to _______.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, I never -- I never seen him. I never seen him. But we used to bum around together, Bob and Otto Furst (ph), Lenny, me, Joe Yost (ph). Joe Yost (ph), he was on a liberty ship. You know -- What the hell do they call these guys? See, that's what happens when you get old. He was a sailor. And he wasn't -- he wasn't in the Navy though, you know. But they'd pay him so much for going over and coming back. Do you realize they could build a ship in so many hours? I was watching that darn thing. I never knew this. I knew it took time. At first it did take time. But, man, did they produce them darn ships, liberty ships. They sent 'em out one after the other, like -- like airplanes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, they send them things out. I never knew that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Kaiser (ph) was building those, right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I never knew that. And, man, they send them suckers out. They put so many on so much -- put it together and, whew, out it would go. And they lost a lot of them too. But they built a lot of them too. That bottom of the ocean must be getting all rusty, huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other strong, vivid memories of missions overseas that we haven't talked about?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Not -- Not -- Not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: _______+_______ in the preview sheets.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: See, take a look through there. I mean.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think we've covered a lot of what we talked about. Oh, yeah, I guess you talked about that. Talk about that again. At one point, you were trying to confuse the radar?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. jiminy ditz, that's something I forgot about. We had -- In order -- In order to confuse the radar, they would send three ships ahead of the outfit and they would throw tinsel, that's what it amounted to, like the tinsel you put on a tree, you know, on the heavy side. And all you did was pull the strap and snap it and it would all start floating down. And then the Germans would pick this up on the radar, and they wouldn't realize that the planes were up above 'em. They figured they were down there where the radar was, so that's what they'd be shooting at. And this one day, we went out in the morning and we had gone on a bomb run, came back, we had chicken ala king and -- well, it was good chicken, like anything else. But I tell you, we got up in the air there; and I had these boxes -- we were flying -- we were flying these fast fighters like this that throw this radar out there; and I had to go so doggone bad I even took off my heavy clothing and I crapped in this box and threw the whole damn box over. But I guess it did good though to -- you know -- the -- it did distract the radar. I'll -- I'll never forget that one. Boy, I -- I -- I didn't care if I died that day. That's how bad I felt. END OF SIDE 1 BEGINNING OF SIDE 2

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And somewhere near Trafalgar Square, we'd try to get in the Royalton (ph) Hotel or something like that and we'd always go in the bars; and this -- this one time, we was -- we was sitting there, drinking, and we had -- we had money. The infantry -- Our infantry had money too but the -- the English, hell, we made more money -- we made more money than their pilots did. And they -- They were a little perturbed about that. They always said, you know, "The Yanks, they're here -- over here, they'd fool around with our _______ and they got the money and they're still over here." But anyway, this -- this -- this one gang, they sat down -- and they were on a submarine; these guys were on a sub -- they had come in and we're shootin' the breeze there, talking; and they commented that they wouldn't want to be in the air; and we commented that we wouldn't want to be down there. At least from up there, we got a chance. They said, no, they stand a better chance. But we bought each -- each other drinks. We were getting pretty well stoned. And some of the boys from the infantry got in on it; and they were arguing about this and arguing about that; a fight ensued. But Mackie (ph), Sam, and I, we took off. We got the heck out of there. That was enough. Did I tell you about this -- Here's a joke. In London, they -- they always got fog; and these prostitutes, they -- they'd stand around the corner, you know; and they'd charge you a pound around the corner, 2 in the taxicab, 3 if you spend the night with them, which is like 4, 8, 12 dollars, right? And this one fella, he was -- he said -- well, he says, he's got a pound, which was $4, and she was standing there, her mascara was running down her and she had a scarf on, you know; so he gets her against the wall, he starts horsin' around with her, and her head keeps bobbing up and down, you know; and she -- he says to her, he says, "Why is your head going up and down?" She says, "You got a bit of me scarf tucked in there." This is true. This is true. At Trafalgar Square, that's the only place where we could get cold beer. Every place else was -- well, it was half and half; but I mean, it was warm beer. That's the way they drank their beer. They liked it that way. But in Trafalgar Square, the -- Chandel's (ph) on Trafalgar Square, they had cold beer. And that's where most of the GIs hung out 'cause they're used to cold beer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were most of the English people nice to you or --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They were very, very nice, really nice. Like when we were stationed in Chelmsford there, we'd go into town and we'd get fish and chips. They'd wrap it up in newspaper. They had newspaper, wrap it up in newspaper, you know. You'd get a couple pieces of fish and some french fries in there. And -- Oh, they -- they were nice. Hell, they'd -- they'd bend over backwards, actually. I mean, in our case they did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Now, how it was otherwise I don't know. But in our case, they -- they took good care of us. They looked after us. We -- Then one time in London, Mac -- Mac was running around with this one English girl. And we went -- It was an air raid; so everybody heads for the tunnel, the down tubes, you know; and he -- he's feeling no pain; and this one girl, she takes -- she takes him, she says, "Come on, I'll take you home," she says, "so you can sleep it off," 'cause we were catching a boat -- a train the next day to head back to Chelmsford. And they -- They -- They took pretty good care of us; really they did. They were nice people -- as long as -- long as -- I don't think you tried to juice 'em or that, you know. Same thing, like when we got over in India -- now, that is another people there again, you know. But they -- They were pretty nice. We had -- We had a boy taking care of our tent for us and we paid him, couldn't have been a hell of a lot, we didn't have that much; but we paid him something; and they were nice. I'll never forget one time, we went to a show when we were in India there, one of these outside things. You -- You sat on sandbags.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And they had the movie going on down; and on the tree going down, we had -- there was -- not bees. What the hell do you call those things? They were like a bee.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Only -- Only they were -- they were -- they were hanging down maybe 2, 3 foot off of the limb of the tree like that. And everybody was going through 'em. Well, this was okay. On the way back, someone gets a bright idea; they start throwing stones -- stones at that thing. Oh, Jesus, if I can only think --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A hornet's nest or a wasp --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, that's it. That's it, yeah. And you should see the guys. These things were all over the place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Woo-hoo, had such a -- actually, you know, you threw -- threw a -- threw a big hole in it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And then these things, they start chasing. Boy, everybody took off. They didn't know where the heck to go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. In -- When we went over, we went to the Ascension Islands from -- from North Carolina, yeah; we flew down to North Carolina; and then from there, we went over to Ascension Islands. We didn't fly in a group. We flew individually because trying to haul the group, you're wasting gas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And Ryerson (ph), on the way over, "Heisan (ph), you know where we're at?" "Yeah, I know where we're at." He's shooting the stars and everything else, you know. "Don't worry, Ry, we're going to get there," he says. I said, "We better because when we get there, we ain't going to have too much gas." And he did, he come right in. He got good. He got damn good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The B26 always had a reputation for being a tough plane to fly.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. They had a hard time when they first learned how to fly them. They -- They're a good, strong plane; but, I don't know, they're temperamental or the pilots were scared of 'em or what, I don't know what the heck it was. But they did have a bad reputation, yeah. We called them the coughing coffins and everything else. But I thought they were a pretty good plane. They brought us back. Oh, then, one time we were shot up pretty bad. I mean, the one engine was gone and it flew pretty good with one engine. We had to get up over -- close to Dover coming back from France. And the wings pretty well shot up and -- it was just a mess; but he did make it over -- made it over. We landed on an English base. Then they flew us back to our base 'cause our plane was in no shape to go anywhere any more. We were lucky. That's exactly what it was. We were lucky. Like the Good Lord said, "I'm going to take care of these dummies."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were hit by flak that time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, that was the biggest --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: That was the biggest concern was the flak.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. I have a note here about targets. Is there something we haven't talked about targets?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, tow targets.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, maybe that's --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Tow targets over -- all over Lake Michigan. Oh, yeah, when we first got together and they had targets, they were towing them out over the Lake, and then the gunners would get a chance to shoot at them. Then they'd see how good you were, you know. And naturally this is all after gunnery school and that; and, boy, every -- I'd go up and flying on top of the water, I'd throw up in my fatigue hat and throw it overboard. And this happened two or three different times. I -- I -- I'd just get nauseous. So the one time I come back, I went to see Doc Mann (ph). I'll never forget him. And he said, "You're scared." I said, "That's right." I knew it, you know. What the hell was I going to do about it? I was scared. But he said, "I'll tell you what, you don't smoke." I said, "Nope." He says, "Get yourself a pack of cigarettes." This is when I started smoking. He said, "Buy a pack of cigarettes, light one up," and he says, "you be watching so you don't burn yourself and you won't be paying any attention to the water down below you." It worked. It worked. That's no lie, I say. And then -- Yeah, these tow targets that they set out for us to shoot at, Mac, he'd shoot at it and Connie, the tail gunner; and then I'd shoot at it. We all had different colored -- see who hit the damn target. That one time -- I forgot about this. That one time -- We had two package -- two guns on the side and in the celle, two .50 caliber machine guns mounted. And our -- our plane, for us, it was fast, 226, you know; it wasn't all that fast, but it was faster than a lot of the planes. And this one day, we were hit by fighters. And this one -- one plane came down and went through and shot -- shot up everything. Didn't knock nothin' down but he -- he started coming back up again after -- he went through and went down, he come back up, going to get the alt -- altitude again and make another pass. Well, Ryerson (ph) took this damn thing, plane, stood it on end down there, started shooting. And then he started running into the bullets that were coming out of the -- out of our plane. He almost got credited with a kill.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And that's no lie.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. But you didn't get them. Arthur W. Gedeon June 9, 2001

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, we didn't get them -- no, he didn't get them. We were lucky. Well, the one time we had fighters and our boys left us, they went to take care of the fighters; and one of the boys was shot up, one of the fighter pilots, his plane was shot up pretty bad; so he -- he came in. He stayed underneath us for cover. And we helped him back. When he got back near the Cliffs of Dover, he took off by himself 'cause he wasn't worried about somebody shooting at him because he couldn't pretty well protect himself. The plane was pretty well shot up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But he made it back. You know, I -- You know, I -- I still feel bad for the 17s and 24s. They -- They had to circle to get altitude because they couldn't just take off and gain the altitude.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Ours -- In our planes, we took off and headed -- headed for the Channel right away and were gaining our altitude as we're going up. These guys had to circle around. And then when they did get up to altitude, they went on oxygen right away, over 10,000 feet. And then there they were for eight hours, or whatever it took 'em, you know. Our planes, we had four hour's fuel consumption; that was it. And, boy, they -- they took -- well, it was the same thing as like the English -- the British -- what the hell they call -- Lancasters? I think that's what they were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: British Lancasters. Man, when we hit that field that time, they had them planes so low, they were all shot up and everything else. They said it was better fighting at night, you know. They flew nights; we flew days. But once -- Once we got the 51 over there, I think that -- that's really the turning point because they could follow -- follow the -- the heavies into the target, follow them back. Prior to that time, they could only go so far and then they were on their own with the fighters; they were on their own with the flak; then down -- on their own again with the fighters coming back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I -- I know we -- we lost a lot of planes from the flak. We -- A couple of our guys -- Well, the one -- the one plane that we were supposed to fly, he got shot up pretty bad. He -- He -- They were all taken prisoners. But that was strictly flak. Most of our --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: -- casualties were flak.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: R & R, shoot rabbits.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were issued a .45. You weren't supposed to do this. And the officers had bikes, so we would borrow their bikes and go out to the countryside. This was England. And -- Well, they had cows, you know, and everything. And these rabbits were out there. We'd take the .45 and, bang, couldn't hit nothin' with the darn thing, but we were making a lot of noise. The cows stopped giving milk. A bulletin board went up, "No shootin' any more." That's no lie. And, you know, we had -- we had honey dumpers out there, they -- they would pick up the crap every so many days. And we had a big -- big tent that had a crapper on each corner of the tent, one in the middle; so you'd sit there and bullshit with this guy while you're going to the john. When we were at -- where the hell was it? Was it in France, England? I think this -- this was stateside. We -- They had the -- the johns there that flushed every once in a while and water just come down from this end and flushed all the johns out. So one time, Mac, he lit a newspaper up on this end; and these guys are sitting on the john; and it flushed -- and the newspaper through there -- and all these Arthur w. Gedeon June 9, 2001 guys, "Whoop, whoop, whoop, whoop." It's funny what you remember, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly. Let's see, did you bring any souvenirs back? Other than the one you gave me?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I had a -- I had a -- Well, I started off -- right after the Bulge, I had a German gun, you know, the big ones that they had. And they took them away from us when we got on the boat. Somebody got 'em, but I don't know who. But I did have a bayonet. I gave that to my son. That's all. No souvenirs. I wasn't in the -- in the souvenirs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This one, KP after tour of duty?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We -- We went to Bournemouth, England. We were waiting for the boat. And ended up on KP; and we weren't supposed to. They -- They have permanent KP, you know. And I -- I got in touch with Ryerson (ph); and I told him, I said, "Ryerson (ph), what the hell's going on here?" I says, "Just because we're laying around getting rest, they put us all on KP." He said, "That can't be." I said, "The hell it ought -- it is." And he went and talked -- I don't know who he talked to but no more KP. He says, "These guys have just come back," he said, "they're lucky to be living and you put them on KP." He said, "You got permanent KP; why don't you use them." I mixed the salad. Did I tell you about that? I had -- I had a ring. And I was mixing the salad and -- you know, the salad's got to be cold; so all the sudden, there's a ring. What the hell? Did I take the ring out? It was my ring! It -- My fingers had gotten so cold that the ring slid off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: But I don't have it any more. I had to get it cut off.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lucky you found it.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, but, I'm trying to think what else. Well, I did see Ryerson (ph). Mae and I, we went to see Ryerson (ph) and his wife in - in Washington. And we went out that night, with my mother watching Artie -- we had Artie with -- Artie then; and my mother watched Artie and we went -- we went bumming. They showed us the sights of Washington. And the following -- following V -- was it the VE-day that they throw the flowers on the graves?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Memorial --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Armistice Day -- Armistice Day. Armistice Day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, you call Armistice Memorial Day.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. He had taken off and one engine quit. He piled into the barracks and got killed. I talked to his wife. She said, "Yeah" -- He was in -- It was in the paper and I called her right away. She said, "Yeah, that's him." So -- Can you imagine? I mean, all this time and he stayed in just, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Well, that's like our Colonel Hall. When you -- When he was flying, we knew we were going to have a pretty rough way to go. And then after that, he stayed in. Well, he was regular Army -- regular. And he -- He got killed overseas, though. Yeah, he got killed overseas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you remember about -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I don't know what time or when.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Ryerson (ph), was that a year or two after the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, about two years afterward, yeah. He -- He stayed in. We -- We talked to each other on the phone and that and -- well, Connie -- Connie and Mackie (ph) and I, then -- then we corresponded quite a bit. We went and visited a couple times each. Then when Connie died -- he died of cancer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: And I'll never forget. He -- He had a bakery -- bakery route out through the country, you know. And if he had day-old cakes or that, all he did was take a little frosting and doctor them up and make them look good. And he always told us this -- he says, "This one farmer woman, she said, 'Sammy,' she says, 'I don't know,' she says, 'but that cake I got the other day,' she said, 'that wasn't as fresh as it's supposed to be.'" He mentioned her by name. He said, "You don't think I would do something like that?" And then he got in on the Charles' Chip -- you know Charles' Chips?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right, right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: He got into that thing. In fact, he gave Mae a Charles' Chip truck.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your entire crew made it through the 66 missions?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yes, we did. No, no, Mackie (ph) didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Other than Mackie (ph).

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Other than Mac, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How -- How many did he make before he was wounded?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: I think it was -- about 61, 62, something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, so he almost made it --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: He almost made it too.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Only -- that one we shot up at, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But he made it back.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: He made -- Oh, yeah, he made it back. He made it back. He -- He met this little girl in London and -- Marie her name was -- and she -- this is the one I was telling you that she took him in the house, you know; and evidently he was fooling around with her 'cause she -- she got quite large; and she got in touch with us and -- when he was in the hospital --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: -- and she says, "What hospital is that?" I says, "All I know is he's in the hospital. I think he's in London. I'm not sure, Marie." She says, "Well, I wanted to talk to him anyhow." But he -- He said she was higher than a kite when he left her.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: So that wasn't good either. Not for her anyhow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you got back?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, I -- Nightmares. I dreamt a lot of bit -- quite a bit. You know, you think your submarine's going down or something like that and you have a fire; and Mae, she'd always wake me up, she says, "You're howling in your sleep again." It wasn't too long, thought, I settled down. What the hell. I had no choice. But there again, like I say, I think the heavies had it hard. Well, even the guys on the ground had it hard too. Let's face it. Everybody had it hard.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the army offer you any counseling at all when you got back?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They just said --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No, we could -- we could go to school on them, you know, if we had wanted to.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But they weren't in the business of dealing with the stress of what you'd --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- been through?

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Not that I know of. I mean --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, I'm not --

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah, not that I know of. I didn't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: _______ experience, I'm sure. That was true of my dad.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Look at him, that poor soul.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Gedeon
sp.p: They say you give it your all. Well, you know, it is -- this is no kiddin', Tom; if they were to put us same as back them years, back in '45 and that, and we were in our 40s, 50s, they'd tell you to do this, and you'd go like this. They wanted kids, and that's exactly what they got. They got kids. Gung-ho. They didn't -- They didn't care. They just wanted to do what they were supposed to do. And -- And Good Lord willing, you did it, you know.
